tldr: By automatically reconstructing a physical digital twin of an articulated door from a single smartphone RGB video and performing imitation learning on trajectories synthesized by an autonomous agent in simulation, a wheel-legged quadruped robot achieved real door opening and traversal (96.6% success rate) without any human demonstrations.
hero_caption: The overall pipeline of Video2DoorTraversal. It consists of three stages: 'DoorTwin', which reconstructs an articulated digital twin from a single RGB video; 'Agentic Generation', which iteratively self-refines trajectories in simulation; and 'ArticuACT', a dual-depth policy that coordinates base and arm control.
overview:
Having a robot open and traverse a door in the real world is an extremely challenging problem where locomotion and manipulation are tightly coupled. Beyond precise handle unlatching, the robot must coordinate its base and arm without collisions while the door panel swings, navigating through a narrow doorway. Traditional learning-based methods have relied on pre-built assets, extensive real-world demonstrations, or prolonged reinforcement learning and real-world adaptation.

To address this, the authors propose Video2DoorTraversal, a Real-to-Sim-to-Real framework that handles the entire pipeline starting from just 'a single RGB video' of the target door captured with a smartphone. First, an instance-aligned articulated door model (DoorTwin) is automatically generated from the video. Next, an LLM/VLM agent engages in trial-and-error inside a physics simulator to automatically synthesize executable expert trajectories. Finally, they train ArticuACT, an imitation learning policy incorporating robot-centric Plücker ray maps and contact state prediction.

Evaluated on a real wheel-legged quadruped robot (Unitree A2-W + Z1 arm), the system achieved a remarkable average success rate of 96.57% across five real doors. Furthermore, it demonstrated an 80.95% zero-shot success rate on unseen doors, smoothly completing the full sequence of approach, unlatching, pushing open, and traversal in an average of only about 13 seconds at high speed.
contributions: Developed DoorTwin, which automatically constructs a simulation-ready model with metric scale geometry, articulated joints, and appearance textures from a single RGB video

Proposed an agentic trajectory generation method that diagnoses simulation failure logs and autonomously refines skill parameters to collect high-quality expert demonstrations without human teleoperation

Built ArticuACT, a dual-depth imitation learning policy that introduces base-frame Plücker ray map conditioning and future interaction state prediction to achieve smooth whole-body coordination between the base and arm
Demonstrated on a wheel-legged quadruped robot a 96.57% success rate across five real doors and an 80.95% zero-shot success rate on unseen doors, all running fully on onboard compute

sections.heading: Why is 'opening and passing through a door' such a high hurdle for robots?
sections.summary: Door traversal by mobile robots is a difficult task requiring simultaneous handle unlatching and tight base-arm coordination in confined spaces. This work proposes Video2DoorTraversal, which recovers an articulated digital twin from a single RGB video, trains policies entirely in simulation, and deploys them to the real robot.
sections.details:
For autonomous mobile robots to operate effectively in human-centric environments, opening and traversing doors is an unavoidable, vital capability. However, unlike isolated sub-tasks such as merely turning a doorknob or pushing an already open door, having a quadruped or wheeled robot traverse a door requires a continuous, contact-rich chain of operations: approaching, unlatching the handle, coordinating base and arm motions while yielding to the restoring force of the door panel, and slipping through the narrow opening without collision.

Prior studies have primarily relied on large-scale simulations using pre-existing 3D models, human teleoperation demonstrations, or reinforcement learning with notoriously difficult reward engineering. Real-to-Sim-to-Real methods reconstructing simulators from videos have also emerged, but most remain limited to rigid-body manipulation with stationary arms. None have automatically reconstructed articulated structures like doors at real-world scale and simulation-ready fidelity to achieve full-body coordinated control.

To overcome this bottleneck, this paper positions door articulation as a unified task representation. The authors established a fully automated pipeline: generating a DoorTwin with accurate dimensions and joints from a single smartphone video, autonomously producing expert data via an agent in simulation, and training the ArticuACT coordination policy powered purely by onboard depth cameras.

captions.F1: Real-world door traversal by a wheel-legged quadruped robot. Using only a single RGB video as input, the robot smoothly and autonomously approaches, unlatches, pushes open, and traverses various office and glass doors.

sections.heading: Limitations of prior work and the necessity of articulation as a common language
sections.summary: Previous door manipulation studies and Real-to-Sim-to-Real techniques were constrained by rigid-only objects or lacked traversal capabilities. This framework uses articulated models as the core to seamlessly connect video reconstruction, trajectory generation, and real-world execution.
sections.details:
Previous research on door manipulation falls into three broad categories: simulation learning, online adaptation, and whole-body control. Frameworks like DoorGym and UniDoorManip learn to open and close articulated objects in simulation, but they assume pre-built assets and do not address door frame navigation. Other approaches have achieved traversal using tactile feedback or reinforcement learning, yet they still depend on procedurally generated doors or demand extra real-world adaptation.

On the other hand, Real-to-Sim-to-Real methods transferring knowledge from real-world observations to simulators (such as HUMAN2SIM2ROBOT and Video2Sim2Real) are powerful for transferring human demonstration videos or object dynamics, but their focus has been rigid manipulation with fixed arms, frequently requiring supplementary 3D scans.

A key distinction of this work lies in unifying the door's articulated structure as a shared task representation across digital twin reconstruction, trajectory generation, and policy execution. It connects simulation construction, data generation, and real deployment end-to-end from a single RGB video without any pre-scanning or manual asset fixing.

sections.heading: Three stages connecting a single video to a real-world policy
sections.summary: The system consists of three stages: DoorTwin construction, agentic trajectory generation, and ArticuACT policy training. Metric reconstruction, self-refining loops in a physics simulator, and Plücker ray maps for geometric grounding serve as key pillars.
sections.details:
The proposed methodology consists of three main stages.

[3.1 DoorTwin: One-Shot Generation of Simulation-Ready Doors]
From a smartphone-recorded video, this stage builds an articulated model (URDF and meshes) that can be imported directly into a physics engine with both appearance and physical properties. First, DAGE estimates camera trajectories and absolute metric depth for each frame (with glass and reflective surfaces corrected by LingBot-Depth). Next, SAM 3 segments the door region across all frames, camera poses are used to fuse point clouds, and Principal Component Analysis (PCA) determines the door normal, width, and height. Furthermore, a VLM selects the optimal reference frame to compute the handle's relative position with respect to the door panel, $\mathbf{p}_{h\mid p} = R_p^T(\mathbf{c}_h - \mathbf{c}_p)$.
These dimensional constraints are passed to a code-generation agent (based on Articraft) to hierarchically instantiate the door frame, panel, revolute joint, and handle. The generated model is rendered from reference viewpoints, where a visual Critic evaluates silhouette alignment and handle orientation/position against the original image, iterating through a prompt feedback loop. Finally, GPT handles delighting, and Tripo 3D applies textures.

[3.2 Agentic Expert Trajectory Generation: Trajectory Synthesis via Simulator]
Expert robot motions are synthesized on the recovered DoorTwin without human demonstrations. The agent instantiates parameterized skill programs (approaching, grasping, handle turning, pushing, traversing) and executes them in parallel at 50 Hz in Isaac Gym. If a rollout fails, logs of joint rotation, collisions, and keyframe snapshots are fed back to the agent to autonomously update the parameters $\eta_j$. Once a skill program succeeds, domain randomizations over robot initial poses, door friction/damping, and camera viewpoints are applied during replay to collect robust expert trajectories.

[3.3 ArticuACT Policy: Dual-Depth Policy for Coordinated Control]
For imitation learning, the authors employ ArticuACT, an extension of the Action Chunking Transformer (ACT). Taking robot state and dual-depth inputs from a head camera (for global context) and a wrist camera (for local views robust to self-occlusions), it predicts an action chunk of length $H=100$ steps (base linear/angular velocity, 6 arm joints, and gripper). Plücker ray maps describing camera rays in the robot base frame are concatenated with depth features, providing accurate spatial perception resilient to viewpoint shake. In addition, an auxiliary prediction task for a 3D future interaction state ('handle contact flag', 'handle turning progress', 'door opening progress') guides the latent features to capture contact transitions.

captions.F2: Overall framework architecture. In Stage 1, geometric constraints are extracted from the real video to generate and refine the DoorTwin with a Critic. In Stage 2, expert demonstrations are automatically synthesized via a simulator self-diagnosis loop. In Stage 3, ArticuACT is trained with Plücker ray maps and contact prediction.

sections.heading: 96.6% success on real hardware: from asset generation to zero-shot traversal
sections.summary: The authors evaluated 20 door asset generations, simulated traversal comparisons, and real-world experiments on a Unitree A2-W + Z1 platform. The method outperformed baselines across geometric accuracy, task success rate, and generalizability to unseen doors.
sections.details:
[Asset Generation Evaluation]
DoorTwin was compared against existing articulated asset generation methods (Articraft, Articulate-Anything, PhysX-Omni) across 20 real doors. DoorTwin achieved top performance across Scale Score (combining width, height, and handle position errors), mask overlap (mIoU), and visual quality (PSNR/LPIPS/VLM scores). Iterative correction by the reference-view Critic proved particularly effective, resolving missing handles, decorative details, and position misalignments.

[Simulated Traversal Performance]
Evaluation across 20 doors over 256 trials each revealed that open-loop Replay and Object-Aware Replay suffered frequent grasp failures. Reinforcement learning (DoorGym) largely failed (1.17% traversal rate) due to the vast exploration space. Compared to point-cloud-based UniDoorManip (31.64%), Diffusion Policy (55.47%), DP3 (53.12%), and Vanilla ACT (69.53%), the proposed ArticuACT achieved an outstanding 99.22% door opening rate and 95.70% traversal success rate.
Ablations showed that combining Plücker conditioning with the auxiliary contact prediction task yielded a 26.18% improvement over Vanilla ACT. Furthermore, direct joint position control demonstrated superior stability during contact and better compatibility with low-level controllers compared to end-effector (EE) control.

[Real-World Experiments and Zero-Shot Generalization]
A Unitree A2-W wheel-legged robot equipped with a Z1 arm and RealSense D435 cameras at the head and wrist ran all inference onboard a Jetson Orin NX. Across five distinct real office doors (including glass and single-leaf doors), the average success rate reached 96.57%. The complete cycle from approach, handle turning, and pushing to traversal took only about 13 seconds on average, operating continuously and smoothly without hesitation.
Remarkably, when a policy trained on one door was deployed directly to three structurally similar unseen real doors, it succeeded in 25/35, 31/35, and 29/35 trials, achieving an impressive zero-shot average success rate of 80.95%.

captions.F3: Qualitative comparison of articulated door asset generation. While existing methods (such as Articulate-Anything and PhysX-Omni) exhibit distorted door proportions and misaligned handles, DoorTwin (Ours) accurately recovers real-world scale and appearance.
captions.F4: The iterative refinement process guided by the reference-view Critic. In the first round, missing handles and door windows are added; in the second and third rounds, their sizes and positions are accurately aligned with the real image.
captions.F6: Real-world rollout snapshots and the trajectory of predicted interaction states. The predictions for handle contact, handle rotation, and door opening progress synchronize perfectly with the physical progression, as forward base velocity ($v_x$) smoothly rises.

sections.heading: Summary and future outlook: expanding from push to pull and varied mechanisms
sections.summary: This work establishes a powerful pipeline that constructs digital twins from a single video and trains base-arm coordinated policies entirely in simulation. Future extensions aim to address pull doors and diverse latching mechanisms.
sections.details:
Video2DoorTraversal constructs simulation-ready door twins from just a single smartphone RGB video, combining agentic expert trajectory synthesis with imitation learning to achieve highly reliable door opening and traversal on a wheel-legged quadruped robot.

In real-world experiments, the framework posted a 96.57% success rate on known doors and 80.95% on unseen similar doors, completing fast-paced operations in approximately 13 seconds entirely on onboard compute.

A current limitation is that the scope is confined to push doors. For future work, the authors plan to expand the framework to pull doors requiring backward coordinated motion, alternative handle types like round knobs, and wider varieties of door architectures.

takeaways: Combining metric 3D reconstruction with a VLM-based visual Critic allows automated creation of physics-simulation-ready articulated digital twins from a single smartphone video.
An agent loop that iteratively diagnoses and corrects simulation rollout failures offers a compelling alternative to expensive human teleoperation demonstrations.

In mobile manipulation, Plücker ray conditioning in the robot base frame combined with auxiliary contact state prediction is decisive for achieving smooth coordination between the mobile base and the arm.
limitations: Supported actions are limited to push doors, lacking trajectory generation and whole-body coordination for doors that must be pulled open toward the robot.
Mechanisms beyond lever handles (such as round knobs, panic push bars, or key-locked latches) have not been extensively evaluated.
Relies on a specialized depth correction module (LingBot-Depth) for glass doors and strong reflections, leaving robustness challenges under extreme lighting variations or specialized materials.
